title: Two months of right iliac fossa pain and loose stools in a 20-year-old university student
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 20-year-old engineering student with 2 months of right iliac fossa pain, loose stools with blood mixed in that wake her at night, mild fevers and unintentional weight loss. She is a social smoker and has recently been taking aspirin. On examination she has right iliac fossa tenderness, perianal inflammation with skin tags and mild finger clubbing. The candidate then interprets her blood, stool and urine results and her colonoscopy and biopsy report, recognises ileocolonic Crohn's disease with perianal disease and iron deficiency anaemia, and plans shared care with gastroenterology, lifestyle changes and safety netting.
focus: Chronic right iliac fossa pain and diarrhoea in a young woman: recognising and managing Crohn's disease
stem: You are a medical student on placement in a metropolitan general practice. The GP has asked you to see the next patient, Beth Bartholomews, a 20-year-old university student who has come in with abdominal pain.
tasks: Take a focused history from Beth and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Beth's results. Hand over to your supervising GP using ISBAR, including your interpretation, give your diagnosis and differentials, then outline your management and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Beth Bartholomews, a 20-year-old engineering student. You are friendly and chatty, a bit tired of the pain, and a little embarrassed talking about your bowels. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "I've had some bad tummy pains which aren't going away."

The pain (give only when asked):

  • Site: the lower right side of your tummy (point to the right iliac fossa). It doesn't go anywhere else.
  • Started about 2 months ago. It hasn't got much better or worse since. You have never had anything like it before.
  • A dull ache, about 5 out of 10.
  • It is there all the time but goes up and down through the day.
  • Nothing makes it better or worse, and eating makes no difference.
  • At first you thought you had eaten something bad.

Bowels (give only when asked):

  • Mild diarrhoea for the same 2 months: loose stools, about 3 or 4 times a day, with some discomfort when you pass them.
  • Lately you sometimes wake at night to go.
  • Sometimes a little blood mixed in with the stool. You haven't noticed any mucus. The colour of your stool hasn't changed.
  • No urgency: you never have to rush to the toilet.
  • No accidents (incontinence) and no constipation. Passing wind normally.
  • Maybe a little bloated.

Other symptoms:

  • Weight: say this only if asked directly: you have lost about 2 kg over the 2 months without trying.
  • Maybe a mild fever at times. No tiredness beyond normal and no night sweats.
  • Appetite normal, no change in your diet.
  • No nausea, vomiting, reflux, trouble swallowing, yellow skin or itch.
  • No joint pain, eye problems, rashes or mouth ulcers.
  • No pain or change when passing urine. You had one urine infection last year, which was treated.
  • No chest pain, breathlessness or cough.
  • No travel, no recent antibiotics, and no one around you has been sick.

Periods and sexual health (give only when asked): last period 2 weeks ago; regular cycle of about 30 days. No vaginal discharge, no pain with sex, no bleeding between periods or after sex, and your periods are not especially painful. You are sexually active with one exclusive partner and always use condoms; you are not on the pill. "There's no way I could be pregnant." You have never had a sexually transmitted infection.

Past medical history: asthma as a child; you haven't needed a puffer for more than 10 years. No operations or hospital admissions. Immunisations up to date.

Medications: you have been taking aspirin recently for headaches from exam stress (a few times a week for the last month or so). Condoms for contraception, not on the pill. No vitamins or supplements.

Allergies: none known.

Family history: your mum has arthritis (you don't know what type) and type 2 diabetes. You have no contact with your father and don't know his side of the family. No brothers or sisters. No one on your mum's side has bowel disease, coeliac disease or bowel cancer that you know of.

Social history:

  • Social smoker: a few cigarettes when you are out with friends.
  • Alcohol about 3 nights a week, 2 to 3 drinks each time.
  • Studying engineering at university; exams have been stressful.
  • You play soccer and netball every week.
  • You eat your mum's cooking and campus food. You live with your mum and have lots of friends.
  • If asked: born and raised in Australia; no known contact with anyone who has had tuberculosis.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Ideas: you first thought it was something you ate, and now wonder whether it is stress from exams.
  • Concerns: it is getting in the way of uni and sport, and you are a bit worried because it isn't going away.
  • Expectations: you want to know what is causing it and get something to fix it.

Question to raise once in Part 1: "Could it just be stress from my exams?"

Exam findings (examiner gives when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: slim, comfortable at rest, alert. Weight 58 kg, height 168 cm, BMI 20.5.
  • Observations: HR 88 regular, BP 112/70, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.6 °C.
  • Hands: mild finger clubbing. No koilonychia, no palmar erythema.
  • Face and eyes: mild conjunctival pallor. No scleral icterus. Eyes not red.
  • Mouth: no aphthous ulcers.
  • Skin and joints: no rashes, no erythema nodosum or pyoderma. Joints not swollen or tender.
  • Neck: no lymphadenopathy.
  • Abdomen: not distended, no scars. Soft. Tender in the right iliac fossa, with no guarding or rebound. No masses felt. Rovsing's and psoas signs negative. No hepatosplenomegaly. Bowel sounds normal. Renal angles not tender. Hernial orifices clear.
  • Perianal inspection and rectal examination (only if the candidate asks for consent and a chaperone): some inflammation around the anus and several small skin tags. No fistula opening, abscess or fissure seen. Rectal examination mildly uncomfortable, no mass; loose brown stool with a streak of blood on the glove.
  • Pelvic examination (if offered): not needed today; say any tests will be discussed in Part 2.
  • Cardiovascular and respiratory: normal.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self as a medical student, confirms Beth's identity and gains consent.
Explains why sensitive questions (bowels, sexual history, alcohol, smoking) are being asked, asks them without judgement, and uses plain language throughout.
History
Characterises the pain:

kids.x: Site and radiation: right iliac fossa, no radiation.
Onset, duration and character: 2 months, never before, constant dull ache fluctuating through the day, 5/10.
Modifying factors: nothing changes it, not related to food; first thought it was something she ate.

check.x: Characterises the change in bowel habit:

kids.x: Loose stools for 2 months, now waking her at night.
Asks specifically about blood (a little, mixed in) and mucus (none), and stool colour.
Discomfort passing stool, urgency or incontinence (none), constipation and flatus.

check.x: Screens for constitutional red flags: asks directly about weight loss (2 kg unintentional over 2 months), fever (maybe mild), night sweats, lethargy and appetite.
Completes the GI review: nausea, vomiting, reflux, dysphagia, jaundice, itch and bloating.
Asks about extraintestinal features of IBD: joint pain, red or painful eyes, rashes and mouth ulcers.
Asks about infective causes: travel, recent antibiotics, sick contacts and diet change.

Takes a gynaecological, sexual and urinary history: LMP 2 weeks ago, regular 30-day cycle, one exclusive partner, condoms, possibility of pregnancy, previous STIs; dysuria or urine change and last year's UTI.
check.d: Award if the candidate covers pregnancy possibility and most of the rest.

check.x: Takes the past medical history: childhood asthma with no puffer for over 10 years, no surgery or admissions, immunisations up to date.
Takes a medication and allergy history and identifies recent aspirin use for exam headaches; condoms only, no supplements; no known allergies.
Takes a family history and asks specifically about IBD, coeliac disease and bowel cancer: mother has arthritis and type 2 diabetes, father's history unknown, no siblings.
Takes a social history: social smoker, alcohol about 3 nights a week at 2 to 3 drinks, engineering student with exam stress, weekly soccer and netball, diet, lives with her mother.
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations and answers her stress question honestly: stress can worsen bowel symptoms, but blood, night-time diarrhoea and weight loss need investigating.
Examination
Asks for vital signs, weight and BMI, and notes the low-grade temperature of 37.6 °C.
Examines the hands and face: finds mild finger clubbing and conjunctival pallor; checks for jaundice and nutritional status.
Looks for extraintestinal manifestations: mouth ulcers, red eyes, erythema nodosum or pyoderma, and swollen joints.

Examines the abdomen: inspection, palpation of all regions (right iliac fossa tenderness without guarding, rebound or mass), appendix signs, liver and spleen, bowel sounds, renal angles and hernial orifices.
Asks for consent and a chaperone for perianal inspection and a rectal examination, finds perianal inflammation and skin tags, and looks specifically for a fistula, abscess or fissure.
Summarises the findings and links them: right iliac fossa tenderness, perianal disease and clubbing point towards inflammatory bowel disease, Crohn's more than ulcerative colitis.
Interpretation
Identifies iron deficiency anaemia: Hb 108, MCV 76, ferritin 9, transferrin saturation 6%, from GI blood loss.
check.d: Optional extra (not required for the mark): inflammation (hepcidin) reduces iron absorption; ferritin is an acute-phase reactant.

check.x: Identifies active inflammation: CRP 36, ESR 38, platelets 462 and neutrophils 7.9, with a low albumin of 33 from inflammation and intestinal loss.
States that negative tTG-IgA with normal total IgA makes coeliac disease unlikely.
check.d: Optional extra (not required for the mark): notes that renal function, LFTs, B12 and folate are normal.

check.x: Interprets the stool tests: calprotectin 820 shows intestinal inflammation and argues against IBS; negative stool PCR, culture and C. difficile toxin make infective colitis unlikely.
check.d: Optional extra (not required for the mark): names Yersinia as an infection that can mimic terminal ileitis.

check.x: Interprets the urine: negative β-hCG excludes pregnancy, including ectopic.
check.d: Optional extra (not required for the mark): a normal dipstick argues against a UTI.

check.x: Interprets the colonoscopy and biopsies:

kids.x: Terminal ileum: cobblestone mucosa, deep longitudinal ulcers and fissures, contact bleeding; caecum and ileocaecal valve: deep linear ulcers with mild valve narrowing.
Skip lesions with normal mucosa between them and a normal rectum (rectal sparing), unlike the continuous disease from the rectum in ulcerative colitis.
Biopsies: non-caseating granulomas with patchy chronic inflammation.
kids.d: Optional extras (not required for the mark): acid-fast bacilli stain negative; no dysplasia.

check.x: Gives the diagnosis as Crohn's disease, ileocolonic, with perianal disease and iron deficiency anaemia, justified by the history, examination and results.
Gives at least three differentials with a feature for or against each (for example ulcerative colitis, infective colitis, coeliac disease, IBS, intestinal TB, appendiceal or gynaecological causes).
Management
Explains the diagnosis in plain words: a long-term inflammatory bowel condition that comes and goes, not caused by stress or food, treatable, and not cancer.
Arranges shared care with gastroenterology:

kids.x: Prompt gastroenterology review to start induction therapy as the specialist directs (for example budesonide for mild to moderate ileocaecal disease, or prednisolone for more active disease).
kids.d: Credit either agent if the candidate defers the choice to the gastroenterologist.

kids.x: States that maintenance therapy and staging (for example MR enterography) will be decided by the gastroenterologist.
kids.d: Credit, but do not require, noting predictors of a more aggressive course (young age at diagnosis, perianal disease (especially fistulising), deep ulceration, extensive disease, steroid need at diagnosis and smoking), or pelvic MRI if a perianal fistula or abscess is suspected.

check.x: Stops aspirin and other NSAIDs because they can trigger flares and cause bleeding; suggests paracetamol for headaches.
Advises stopping smoking completely, explaining that smoking worsens Crohn's disease (more flares and surgery), and offers support (brief advice, Quitline 13 7848).
Treats the iron deficiency (IV iron is preferred while the disease is active; oral iron, for example on alternate days, is acceptable if tolerated) and plans to recheck FBC and iron studies.
States that infection screening and a vaccination review are needed before immunosuppression, and raises reliable contraception.
Addresses nutrition (dietitian, weight) and wellbeing (stress support, Crohn's & Colitis Australia, keep alcohol low).
check.d: Award for any one of: dietitian, stress or university support, Crohn's & Colitis Australia, keeping alcohol low.

check.x: Safety netting

Tells her to go to the ED or call 000 for severe or worsening constant pain, vomiting with a swollen tummy or not passing wind, heavy bleeding, feeling faint, high fever, or a painful swelling or discharge around the bottom.
Tells her to contact the GP or IBD nurse the same day for a flare (more frequent stools, more blood, waking at night), new joint, eye or skin problems, or side effects of treatment.
Arranges follow-up: GP review in 2 to 4 weeks (FBC); repeat iron studies no sooner than 4 weeks after IV iron (or after about 4 to 8 weeks of oral iron); confirmed gastroenterology appointment.
check.d: Optional extras (not required for the mark): smoking cessation follow-up; a screening colonoscopy about 8 years after symptoms began.

part2.lead: At the first visit the GP arranged blood, stool and urine tests and referred Beth to a gastroenterologist, who performed a colonoscopy 3 weeks later. Beth has come back today to discuss the results. Here they are.
part2.patient:
Ask these questions once each while the candidate explains the plan:

  • "So is this because of my exam stress?"
  • "I only smoke on nights out. Does that really matter?"
  • "Will I need an operation?"

You are shocked to hear you have a long-term condition but relieved to have an answer. If the candidate uses jargon such as "Crohn's", "immunosuppression" or "biologic" without explaining it, ask what it means.

handover.label: Blood tests
handover.model:
• Read: Hb 108 with MCV 76 and MCH 24 is a microcytic anaemia; ferritin 9, iron 6, transferrin saturation 6% and a high transferrin confirm iron deficiency. CRP 36, ESR 38, platelets 462 and neutrophils 7.9 are raised. Albumin 33 is low. Renal function, LFTs, B12 and folate are normal. tTG-IgA is negative with a normal total IgA.
  • For Beth: iron deficiency from blood loss, with inflammation (hepcidin) reducing iron absorption, alongside active systemic inflammation. Ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so a ferritin this low despite inflammation is clear-cut. Low albumin reflects inflammation and protein loss from the gut. Coeliac disease is unlikely because she is eating gluten and her IgA is normal (so the test is valid).
  • What it changes: she needs iron replacement and repeat bloods. The inflammatory markers support an organic cause and give a baseline to track treatment.

labs.title: Full blood count and inflammatory markers
Electrolytes, urea, creatinine and liver function

handover.label: Stool tests
handover.result: Stool sample collected at the first visit, before colonoscopy. No antibiotics in the previous 3 months.
handover.model:
• Read: faecal calprotectin 820 µg/g, more than 15 times the upper limit. Loose, blood-stained stool with leucocytes and red cells. Bacterial and parasite PCR, culture and C. difficile toxin all negative.
  • For Beth: there is real inflammation in the bowel wall, so this is not IBS. Infective colitis is unlikely, including Yersinia, which can cause right iliac fossa pain and terminal ileitis that mimics Crohn's disease, and C. difficile.
  • What it changes: a raised calprotectin supports the urgency of the gastroenterology referral and colonoscopy. Excluding infection matters before steroids or immunosuppression. Calprotectin will be repeated to track her response to treatment.

rows.t: Bacterial PCR (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia, STEC)

handover.label: Urine tests
handover.result: Point-of-care tests in the practice at the first visit.
handover.model:
• Read: urine β-hCG negative; dipstick negative for leucocytes, nitrites, blood and protein.
  • For Beth: pregnancy, including ectopic pregnancy, is excluded as a cause of right iliac fossa pain, and a urinary tract infection is unlikely.
  • What it changes: pregnancy-related causes, including ectopic pregnancy, are excluded and a UTI is unlikely. Other gynaecological causes (ovarian cyst, PID, endometriosis) are not excluded by these tests but are made unlikely by the history and fully explained by the colonoscopy findings. Offer chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT as routine screening for her age. A negative pregnancy test is also relevant to treatment planning; pregnancy will be re-tested before teratogenic drugs such as methotrexate, and it opens a conversation about reliable contraception.

handover.label: Colonoscopy and biopsy report
handover.result:
Procedure: colonoscopy to the terminal ileum under sedation, 3 weeks after the first visit. Bowel preparation good.

Clinical details: 20-year-old woman with 2 months of right iliac fossa pain, nocturnal diarrhoea with blood, 2 kg weight loss, perianal skin tags and finger clubbing. Faecal calprotectin 820 µg/g; stool pathogens negative.

Findings:

  • Perianal: several small skin tags with mild perianal erythema. No external fistula opening.
  • Rectum: normal vascular pattern, no inflammation (rectal sparing).
  • Sigmoid and descending colon: normal.
  • Transverse colon: a single 4 cm patch of small aphthous ulcers with normal mucosa on either side.
  • Ascending colon: normal.
  • Caecum and ileocaecal valve: patchy deep linear ulcers; the valve is ulcerated and mildly narrowed but the scope passes easily.
  • Terminal ileum (15 cm examined): segmental cobblestone mucosa with deep longitudinal ulcers and fissures; the mucosa bleeds on contact.

Histology (terminal ileum, caecum, transverse colon, rectum): terminal ileum, caecum and transverse colon show patchy chronic active inflammation with crypt architectural distortion, deep fissuring ulceration and non-caseating epithelioid granulomas with multinucleated giant cells. Ziehl-Neelsen stain for acid-fast bacilli negative. No dysplasia or malignancy. Rectal biopsies within normal limits. Mucosal biopsies cannot assess the full thickness of the bowel wall; the deep fissuring ulcers suggest transmural disease.

Conclusion: findings consistent with Crohn's disease involving the terminal ileum and caecum, with a skip lesion in the transverse colon and perianal skin tags. Recommend MR enterography, with pelvic MRI if a perianal fistula or abscess is suspected; gastroenterology clinic review to start treatment.
handover.model:
• Read: terminal ileum: cobblestone mucosa, deep longitudinal ulcers and fissures, contact bleeding; caecum and ileocaecal valve: deep linear ulcers with mild valve narrowing; a separate patch of aphthous ulcers in the transverse colon with normal mucosa between (skip lesions); normal rectum. Biopsies show patchy chronic active inflammation and non-caseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells, no acid-fast bacilli and no dysplasia.
  • For Beth: ileocolonic Crohn's disease with perianal involvement. Skip lesions, rectal sparing, ileal disease, fissures (suggesting transmural inflammation) and granulomas separate it from ulcerative colitis, which is continuous from the rectum and confined to the mucosa. Negative AFB staining and the absence of caseation argue against intestinal TB.
  • What it changes: she needs induction therapy and a maintenance plan with gastroenterology. Young age at diagnosis, perianal disease (especially fistulising), deep ulceration, extensive disease, steroid need at diagnosis and smoking predict a more aggressive course, favouring early immunomodulator therapy, with biologics per PBS criteria if needed. Staging imaging as the specialist arranges: MR enterography for small bowel disease (strictures, fistulas); pelvic MRI if a perianal fistula or abscess is suspected.

ask: You are now calling your supervising GP. Please give an ISBAR handover of Beth Bartholomews, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Beth is with you. Explain her diagnosis and your management plan to her, here in general practice.
Before Beth goes home, what would you tell her and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student; Beth Bartholomews, 20.
  • Situation: colonoscopy confirms Crohn's disease; she needs a treatment plan.
  • Background: 2 months RIF pain, nocturnal bloody loose stools, 2 kg weight loss; smoker, recent aspirin; RIF tenderness, perianal skin tags, clubbing.
  • Assessment: Hb 108, MCV 76, ferritin 9: iron deficiency anaemia from blood loss. CRP 36, platelets 462, albumin 33: active inflammation. Calprotectin 820: bowel inflammation, not IBS; stool PCR, culture and C. difficile toxin negative: infection unlikely. tTG-IgA negative with normal IgA: coeliac unlikely. β-hCG negative: not pregnant. Colonoscopy: ileal and caecal cobblestoning, skip lesions, rectal sparing; non-caseating granulomas, AFB negative, no dysplasia: ileocolonic Crohn's with perianal disease.
  • Recommendation: prompt gastroenterology review to start induction; stop aspirin; iron; smoking cessation; pre-immunosuppression screen.

Most likely: ileocolonic Crohn's disease with perianal disease and iron deficiency anaemia: chronic right iliac fossa pain, nocturnal bloody diarrhoea, weight loss, fever, perianal skin tags, clubbing, smoker; calprotectin 820; cobblestoning, skip lesions and granulomas.

  • Ulcerative colitis: bloody diarrhoea; against: rectal sparing, ileal disease, skip lesions, granulomas, perianal disease.
  • Infective colitis (Yersinia, Campylobacter): started like food poisoning; against: 2 months, stool PCR, culture and C. difficile toxin negative.
  • Intestinal TB: granulomas, ileocaecal disease; against: non-caseating, AFB negative, no TB risk factors.
  • Coeliac disease: diarrhoea, iron deficiency; against: blood, normal tTG-IgA with normal IgA.
  • IBS: exam stress, bloating; against: nocturnal symptoms, blood, weight loss, raised calprotectin.
  • Appendiceal or gynaecological cause: right iliac fossa pain; against: no peritonism over 2 months, negative hCG, no gynaecological symptoms, and colonoscopy findings explain the pain.

1. Explain Crohn's in plain words: long-term bowel inflammation that comes and goes; stress does not cause it but can worsen symptoms; treatable, not cancer.
  2. Gastroenterology shared care: prompt gastroenterology review to start induction (for example budesonide or prednisolone, as the specialist directs); maintenance and staging decided by the specialist. With colonic extension beyond the right colon, moderate activity or high-risk features, the gastroenterologist may prefer prednisolone (for example 40 mg daily, tapered) with an early immunomodulator.
  3. Stop aspirin and NSAIDs; paracetamol for headaches.
  4. Stop smoking completely: it worsens Crohn's; brief advice, Quitline 13 7848, consider NRT.
  5. Iron: IV iron preferred while active; oral iron (for example alternate days) if tolerated; recheck FBC.
  6. Before immunosuppression: infection screen, vaccine review, reliable contraception.
  7. Nutrition and wellbeing: dietitian; stress support, Crohn's & Colitis Australia; keep alcohol low.

• Go to the ED or call 000 for severe or constant worsening pain, vomiting with a swollen tummy or not passing wind (blockage), heavy bleeding or feeling faint, high fever, or a painful swelling or discharge near the bottom (abscess or fistula).
  • Contact the GP or IBD nurse the same day for a flare (more stools, more blood, waking at night), new joint, eye or skin problems, or treatment side effects.
  • Operation question: many people with Crohn's need surgery at some stage, mainly for complications such as narrowing; good treatment and not smoking lower the chance.
  • Follow-up: GP review in 2 to 4 weeks (FBC); repeat iron studies no sooner than 4 weeks after IV iron (or after about 4 to 8 weeks of oral iron); confirmed gastroenterology appointment; quit support; a screening colonoscopy about 8 years after symptoms began will decide whether regular bowel cancer surveillance is needed. Written information.

ddx.dx: Crohn's disease, ileocolonic, with perianal disease
ddx.for: Two months of right iliac fossa pain, nocturnal diarrhoea with blood, weight loss, perianal inflammation with skin tags, clubbing, a smoker, calprotectin 820, and cobblestoning with skip lesions and granulomas at colonoscopy.
Loose stools with blood that wake her at night and a raised calprotectin.
ddx.against: Right iliac fossa pain, perianal skin tags, terminal ileal disease, skip lesions with rectal sparing, and granulomas on biopsy.

ddx.dx: Infective colitis or gastroenteritis (including Yersinia ileitis)
ddx.for: She first thought she had eaten something bad, has loose bloody stools and mild fevers, and Yersinia can mimic terminal ileitis.
ddx.against: Symptoms for 2 months with no travel, antibiotics or sick contacts, and negative stool PCR, culture and C. difficile toxin.

ddx.for: Granulomas and ileocaecal disease with fever and weight loss.
ddx.against: The granulomas are non-caseating, the acid-fast bacilli stain is negative, and she has no TB risk factors.

ddx.for: Diarrhoea, bloating, weight loss and iron deficiency.
ddx.against: Blood in the stool and a negative tTG-IgA with a normal total IgA while eating gluten.

ddx.for: A young woman with exam stress and bloating.
ddx.against: Nocturnal diarrhoea, blood, weight loss, fever, clubbing, and raised calprotectin and CRP.

guide:
This is a GP station with no observation chart: give the observations from the Exam findings when the candidate asks. In Part 1 the patient answers the history, giving the 2 kg weight loss only if asked directly. The examiner gives examination findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. Give the perianal and rectal findings only if the candidate asks for consent and a chaperone. If the candidate offers a pelvic examination, say it is not needed today. If they ask for tests in Part 1, say these will be discussed in Part 2. Whatever the candidate planned, the bloods, stool and urine tests were done at the first visit and the colonoscopy 3 weeks later. In Part 2 hand over all four results, then ask the four questions in order. For Q3 and Q4 the candidate speaks to Beth (the role-player); the examiner marks from what they say to her. Beth asks her three questions once each during the management and follow-up answers.

A high-performing candidate characterises the pain and the bowel change, asks specifically about blood, nocturnal symptoms and weight loss, covers the gynaecological, urinary and infective causes, picks up the aspirin and smoking, and asks about a family history of IBD. They examine for clubbing, pallor and extraintestinal signs, examine the abdomen properly and offer a chaperoned perianal examination. In Part 2 they identify iron deficiency anaemia and active inflammation, use calprotectin and the negative stool tests to rule out IBS and infection, read the colonoscopy and biopsies as Crohn's disease rather than ulcerative colitis, and plan shared care with gastroenterology. Their plan stops the aspirin and the smoking, replaces iron, prepares her for immunosuppression and gives specific red flags for obstruction, perforation and perianal abscess.

A borderline candidate takes a generic pain history without asking about blood, night-time symptoms or weight, omits the sexual and pregnancy history, does not examine the perianal area, calls the anaemia "low iron" without linking it to the disease, cannot separate Crohn's disease from ulcerative colitis, or misses the aspirin and smoking. Accept any reasonable induction approach that defers to the gastroenterologist; candidates are not expected to choose the maintenance drug.
explain:
Diagnosis

Beth has Crohn's disease involving the terminal ileum and caecum, with a skip lesion in the transverse colon, perianal disease and iron deficiency anaemia. Crohn's disease is a chronic, relapsing, transmural inflammatory disease that can affect any part of the gut from mouth to anus, most often the terminal ileum. It commonly presents between 15 and 30 years of age. The history (2 months of right iliac fossa pain, loose stools with blood that wake her at night, weight loss, mild fevers), the examination (right iliac fossa tenderness, perianal inflammation with skin tags, finger clubbing), her smoking and the results all fit.

Approaching abdominal pain in a young woman

Use reading time to list differentials by demographic and region and plan which systems to review: GI, genitourinary, reproductive, haematological, and infective or constitutional (B) symptoms. Then cover UTI and STI risk, travel and contacts, smoking, NSAIDs, stress, past surgery and a family history of IBD.

RegionCauses to consider
Right upper quadrantCholecystitis, cholangitis, hepatitis
EpigastricPeptic ulcer, GORD, pancreatitis
Left upper quadrantSplenic causes
FlanksRenal stones, pyelonephritis
CentralEarly appendicitis, gastroenteritis, obstruction, IBD
Right iliac fossaAppendicitis, ovarian cyst, ovarian torsion, PID, ectopic pregnancy, endometriosis, IBD
SuprapubicUTI

Chronic diarrhoea with blood, nocturnal symptoms, weight loss or fever is organic until proven otherwise. Recent aspirin use is also a reason to consider peptic ulceration and NSAID-related bleeding.

Crohn's disease versus ulcerative colitis

Crohn's diseaseUlcerative colitis
DistributionAnywhere mouth to anus; skip lesions; rectum often sparedRectum, extending continuously proximally; colon only
DepthTransmuralMucosal
EndoscopyCobblestoning, deep linear ulcers, fissures, contact bleedingContinuous erythema, friability, loss of vascular pattern
HistologyPatchy inflammation, non-caseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cellsDiffuse mucosal inflammation, crypt abscesses, no granulomas
Perianal disease, fistulas, stricturesCommonUncommon
SmokingRisk factor; worsens the courseInversely associated (ex-smokers at higher risk); smoking is still not recommended

Mucosal biopsies cannot show full-thickness (transmural) inflammation; that is seen on resection specimens. Deep fissuring ulcers suggest it. Granulomas are found in only a minority of Crohn's biopsies, so their absence does not exclude it. Caseating granulomas or acid-fast bacilli would point to intestinal TB, an important mimic that must be excluded before immunosuppression; Beth's granulomas are non-caseating, the AFB stain is negative and she has no TB risk factors.

Interpreting the results

  • Bloods: microcytic anaemia with ferritin 9 and transferrin saturation 6% is iron deficiency from blood loss, with inflammation (hepcidin) reducing iron absorption. Ferritin rises with inflammation, so in active IBD a ferritin under about 100 can still mean iron deficiency; here it is unequivocal. Raised CRP, ESR, platelets and neutrophils and a low albumin show active inflammation. Other causes of anaemia in Crohn's are B12 deficiency (terminal ileal disease or resection) and anaemia of chronic disease.
  • Coeliac serology: negative tTG-IgA is valid only with a normal total IgA and a gluten-containing diet, both present here.
  • Faecal calprotectin: a neutrophil protein that marks intestinal inflammation. A high value separates IBD from IBS and justifies colonoscopy; it is also used to monitor treatment response.
  • Stool tests: infection, including Yersinia (which causes terminal ileitis) and C. difficile, must be excluded before diagnosing IBD and starting steroids.
  • Urine: a negative β-hCG excludes pregnancy and ectopic pregnancy. It does not exclude other gynaecological causes (ovarian cyst, PID, endometriosis); in Beth these are made unlikely by the history and the colonoscopy explains her pain.

Complications of Crohn's disease

  • Intestinal: strictures and obstruction (inflammation or fibrosis), perforation, fistulas (enteroenteric, enterovesical, enterovaginal, perianal), abscesses, colorectal cancer in colonic disease, and small bowel cancer.
  • Nutritional: malabsorption and malnutrition, iron deficiency anaemia, B12 deficiency, bile acid diarrhoea, gallstones and renal oxalate stones after ileal disease or resection, and reduced bone density.
  • Extraintestinal: arthritis, uveitis and episcleritis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, aphthous ulcers, venous thromboembolism, and rarely amyloidosis.

Management (eTG: Inflammatory bowel disease, Crohn disease)

  • Shared care with a gastroenterologist, with treatment matched to the site, severity and risk of the disease. Staging imaging is arranged by the specialist: MR enterography for small bowel disease, and pelvic MRI if a perianal fistula or abscess is suspected.
  • Inducing remission: oral budesonide (9 mg daily) for mild to moderate ileocaecal disease; systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone) for moderate to severe disease, tapered off. With colonic extension beyond the right colon, moderate activity or high-risk features, the gastroenterologist may prefer prednisolone (for example 40 mg daily, tapered) with an early immunomodulator. Beth has a transverse colon skip lesion, moderate activity (fever, weight loss, CRP 36, albumin 33, Hb 108) and high-risk features, so prednisolone is a likely choice. Steroids are not used for maintenance. Aminosalicylates have little role in Crohn's disease.
  • Maintaining remission: thiopurines (azathioprine or mercaptopurine, after TPMT testing), methotrexate, or biologics (anti-TNF agents, vedolizumab, ustekinumab) under specialist care. Young age at diagnosis, perianal disease (especially fistulising), deep ulceration, extensive disease, steroid need at diagnosis and smoking predict a more aggressive course and favour early immunomodulator therapy, with biologics per PBS criteria if needed.
  • Before immunosuppression: screen for hepatitis B and C, HIV, latent TB and varicella and measles immunity; give non-live vaccines (influenza, pneumococcal, HPV, hepatitis B if not immune), and avoid live vaccines once immunosuppressed. If she is not immune, give live vaccines (MMR, varicella) at least 4 weeks before starting immunosuppression; COVID-19 vaccination should also be up to date. Methotrexate is teratogenic, so reliable contraception is needed; pregnancy is best planned when the disease is in remission.
  • Iron replacement: IV iron is preferred while the disease is clinically active, because inflammation (hepcidin) limits oral absorption and oral iron can worsen GI symptoms. Oral iron (for example on alternate days) is acceptable in mild disease if tolerated. Recheck the FBC in 2 to 4 weeks; ferritin and transferrin saturation are falsely raised for about 4 weeks after an IV iron infusion, so repeat iron studies no sooner than 4 weeks after IV iron (or after about 4 to 8 weeks of oral iron).
  • Surgery is for complications (strictures, abscesses, fistulas, perforation) or disease that does not respond to medical treatment; it is not curative.

Lifestyle

  • Stop smoking: the most important modifiable factor. Smoking increases flares, the need for surgery and recurrence after surgery. Offer brief advice, Quitline and pharmacotherapy.
  • Avoid NSAIDs, including aspirin: they can trigger flares and cause GI bleeding.
  • Nutrition: dietitian input to prevent malnutrition and support weight; calcium and vitamin D, with bone health monitoring, if she has steroids.
  • Stress management and psychological support: stress does not cause Crohn's but can worsen symptoms and coping; link her with university support services and Crohn's & Colitis Australia. Keep alcohol low.

Safety netting and follow-up

Beth should go to the ED for features of obstruction (vomiting, distension, not passing wind), perforation or a severe flare (severe constant pain, high fever, heavy bleeding, feeling faint) or a perianal abscess (painful swelling or discharge). She should contact her GP or IBD nurse for a milder flare, new extraintestinal symptoms or treatment side effects. Review her in 2 to 4 weeks with an FBC, repeat iron studies no sooner than 4 weeks after IV iron, confirm the gastroenterology appointment, and explain that a screening colonoscopy about 8 years after symptoms began will decide whether regular bowel cancer surveillance is needed; ongoing surveillance applies when the colitis is extensive.
points: Chronic diarrhoea with blood, nocturnal symptoms, weight loss or fever is organic until proven otherwise; ask about each directly, along with NSAIDs, smoking and a family history of IBD.
In a young woman with right iliac fossa pain, always take a menstrual, sexual and urinary history and check a pregnancy test.
Right iliac fossa pain, perianal disease and clubbing point to Crohn's disease. Skip lesions, rectal sparing, cobblestoning, fissures and non-caseating granulomas separate it from ulcerative colitis.
Faecal calprotectin separates inflammatory from functional bowel disease, and stool tests must exclude infection (including Yersinia and C. difficile) before IBD is diagnosed and steroids started.
Crohn's disease is managed with a gastroenterologist: steroids induce remission, and immunomodulators or biologics maintain it. Screen for infection and update vaccines before immunosuppression.

Stopping smoking is the most important lifestyle change in Crohn's disease. Also stop NSAIDs, replace iron, support nutrition and stress management, and teach red flags for obstruction, perforation and perianal abscess.
